questions.question: The eigen values of the following matrix are \[\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 & 5 \\ -3 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\]
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of a square matrix \(A\) is obtained by solving the determinant equation: \[|A - \lambda I| = 0\] \[(3 - \lambda)(\lambda^{2} + 2\lambda + 10) = 0\]
  1. \(3 - \lambda = 0 \implies \lambda_{1} = 3\)
  2. \(\lambda^{2} + 2\lambda + 10 = 0\)
Solving the quadratic equation: \[\lambda = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{2^{2} - 4(1)(10)}}{2(1)}\] \[\lambda = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 40}}{2}\] \[\lambda = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{-36}}{2}\] \[\lambda = \frac{-2 \pm 6j}{2} = -1 \pm 3j\] Thus, the eigenvalues of the matrix are \(3\), \(-1 + 3j\), and \(-1 - 3j\). \[\boxed{\text{(D) 3, $-1+3j$, $-1-3j$}}\]

questions.question: The Taylor series expansion of \(\dfrac{\sin x}{x - \pi}\) at \(x = \pi\) is given by
questions.explanation: Given function: \[f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x - \pi} \quad \text{about } x = \pi\] To find the series expansion about \(x = \pi\), let us introduce a temporary variable \(t\): \[\text{Let } x - \pi = t \implies x = \pi + t\] Substitute \(x = \pi + t\) into the function: \[f(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi + t)}{t}\] Using the trigonometric identity \(\sin(\pi + t) = -\sin t\): \[f(x) = \frac{-\sin t}{t}\] Now, substitute the standard Maclaurin series expansion for \(\sin t\): \[\sin t = t - \frac{t^3}{3!} + \frac{t^5}{5!} - \dots\] Thus, the expression becomes: \[f(x) = -\frac{1}{t} \left[ t - \frac{t^3}{3!} + \frac{t^5}{5!} - \dots \right]\] \[f(x) = -1 + \frac{t^2}{3!} - \frac{t^4}{5!} + \dots\] Substituting back \(t = x - \pi\): \[f(x) = -1 + \frac{(x - \pi)^2}{3!} - \frac{(x - \pi)^4}{5!} + \dots\] Hence, the correct option is (d). \[\boxed{\text{(d)}\ \ -1 + \frac{(x - \pi)^2}{3!} - \frac{(x - \pi)^4}{5!} + \dots}\]

questions.question: The order of the differential equation \[\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\right)^3+y^4=e^{-t}\ \ \text{is}\]
questions.explanation:
Given differential equation is \[\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^3 + y^4 = e^{-t}\] The order of a differential equation is defined as the order of the highest derivative present in the equation. Let us identify the derivatives appearing in the given equation:
  • Although the first derivative appears with power \(3\), \(\left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^3,\) its order remains \(1\), because order depends on the derivative itself, not on the power to which it is raised.
  • Similarly, \(y^4\) contains no derivative and therefore does not affect the order.
The highest-order derivative present is \[\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}\] Hence, \[\text{Order of the differential equation} = 2.\] \[\boxed{\text{(B)}\ 2}\]
Key points
  • Order of a differential equation = order of the highest derivative present.
  • The power of a derivative does not affect the order.
  • Terms without derivatives do not contribute to the order.

questions.question:
Match each differential equation in Group I to its family of solution curves from Group II.
Group IGroup II
P.\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x}\)1.Circles
[2ex] Q.\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{y}{x}\)2.Straight lines
[2ex] R.\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x}{y}\)3.Hyperbolas
[2ex] S.\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}\)
questions.explanation:
To identify the family of curves corresponding to each differential equation, solve them one by one and compare the resulting curve with the given families. For \(P\):
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x}\] Separating variables and Integrating, \[\int \frac{dy}{y} = \int \frac{dx}{x}\] \[\ln y = \ln x + C\] \[y = Cx\] This represents a family of straight lines passing through the origin. \[P \rightarrow 2\] For \(Q\):
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}\] Separating variables and Integrating, \[\int \frac{dy}{y} = \int-\frac{dx}{x}\] \[\ln y = -\ln x + C\] \[\ln(xy) = C\] \[xy = C_1\] This is a rectangular hyperbola. \[Q \rightarrow 3\] For \(R\):
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x}{y}\] Separating variables and Integrating, \[\int y\,dy = \int x\,dx\] \[\frac{y^2}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2}+C\] \[y^2-x^2 = C_1\] This is a hyperbola. \[R \rightarrow 3\] For \(S\):
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}\] Separating variables and Integrating, \[\int y\,dy = \int -x\,dx\] \[\frac{y^2}{2} = -\frac{x^2}{2} + C\] \[x^2 + y^2 = C_1\] This represents a family of circles centered at the origin. \[S \rightarrow 1\] Hence, \[P\rightarrow 2,\qquad Q\rightarrow 3,\qquad R\rightarrow 3,\qquad S\rightarrow 1\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)\ P-2,\ Q-3,\ R-3,\ S-1}}\]

questions.question:
A discrete random variable \(X\) takes values from \(1\) to \(5\) with probabilities as shown in the table. A student calculates the mean of \(X\) as \(3.5\) and her teacher calculates the variance of \(X\) as \(1.5\). Which of the following statements is true? \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
k & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\
\hline
P(X=k) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\
\hline
\end{array}\]
options: Both the student and the teacher are right
Both the student and the teacher are wrong
The student is wrong but the teacher is right
The student is right but the teacher is wrong
questions.explanation:
Given probability distribution: \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
k & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5\\
\hline
P(X=k) & 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.2 & 0.1
\end{array}\] Mean of \(X\): \[E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)\] \[E(X)=1(0.1)+2(0.2)+3(0.4)+4(0.2)+5(0.1)\] \[E(X)=0.1+0.4+1.2+0.8+0.5=3\] Hence, the student's answer \(3.5\) is wrong. Now, \[E(X^2)=\sum x^2P(X=x)\] \[E(X^2)=1^2(0.1)+2^2(0.2)+3^2(0.4)+4^2(0.2)+5^2(0.1)\] \[E(X^2)=0.1+0.8+3.6+3.2+2.5=10.2\] Variance: \[\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2\] \[\text{Var}(X)=10.2-3^2\] \[\text{Var}(X)=10.2-9=1.2\] Hence, the teacher's answer \(1.5\) is also wrong. \[\boxed{\text{(b) Both the student and the teacher are wrong}}\]

questions.question: A fully charged mobile phone with a \(12\text{ V}\) battery is good for a \(10\text{ minute}\) talk-time. Assume that, during the talk-time the battery delivers a constant current of \(2\text{ A}\) and its voltage drops linearly from \(12\text{ V}\) to \(10\text{ V}\) as shown in the figure. How much energy does the battery deliver during this talk-time?
questions.explanation: The power delivered by the battery is \[p(t)=v(t)\,i(t)\] Given that the current is constant, \[i(t)=2~\text{A}\] and the voltage decreases linearly from \(12\text{ V}\) to \(10\text{ V}\) in \[T=10~\text{min}=600~\text{s}.\] The energy delivered by the battery is \[E=\int_0^T p(t)\,dt = \int_0^{600} v(t)i(t)\,dt\] \[E = 2\int_0^{600} v(t)\,dt\] The integral of voltage with respect to time equals the area under the \(v\)-\(t\) graph. The area under the graph consists of: \[A_1 = 10\times600 = 6000, \qquad A_2 = \frac12(12-10)\times600 = 600.\] Therefore, \[E = 2(A_1+A_2)= 13200~\text{J} = 13.2~\text{kJ}.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }13.2~\text{kJ}}\]

Let the current through the \(60\text{ V}\) source be \(I_1\) as shown downward through the source. Applying KCL at node \(a\), \[I+I_1-12=0 \ \Rightarrow \ I=12-I_1\] Since the \(60\text{ V}\) source is absorbing power, \[I_1 > 0\] Therefore, \[I<12~\text{A}\] Therefore, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }10~\text{A}}\]

questions.question: The switch in the circuit shown was on a position a for a long time, and is moved to position '\(b\)' at time \(t = 0\). The current \(i(t)\) for \(t > 0\) is given by
questions.explanation: The capacitor network can be simplified as The capacitor current is given by, \(i(t) = i(\infty) + \left[i(0^+)-i(\infty)\right] e^{-t/\tau}\) At \(t=0^-\), the switch is at position \(a\) for a long time. Hence, the capacitor behaves as an open circuit. Therefore, \(V_C(0^-)=100~\text{V}\) Since capacitor voltage is continuous, \(V_C(0^+)=100~\text{V}\) At \(t=0\), the switch is moved to position \(b\). The time constant is , \(\tau = RC = 5\times10^3\times0.16\times10^{-6} = 0.8\times10^{-3}~\text{s}\) At \(t=0^+\); \[i(0^+)=\frac{100}{5k}= 20~\text{mA}\] At \(t\rightarrow\infty\), the capacitor behaves as an open circuit. Hence, \(i(\infty)=0\) Substituting, \[i(t) = 20e^{-t/(0.8\times10^{-3})} = 20e^{-1250t}\,u(t)\ \text{mA}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }20e^{-1250t}u(t)\ \text{mA}}\]

Also, the inductor behaves as a short circuit. Therefore, \[i(\infty) = \frac{V_0}{R}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }\dfrac{V_0}{R}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A function is given by \(f(t) = \sin^2 t + \cos 2t\). Which of the following is true ?
questions.explanation:
Given the function: \[f(t) = \sin^2 t + \cos 2t\] To determine the frequency components, we first express the function in terms of linear sinusoidal functions without powers. We use the standard trigonometric identity: \[\sin^2 t = \frac{1 - \cos 2t}{2} = 0.5 - 0.5\cos 2t\] Substituting this back into the original equation for \(f(t)\): \[f(t) = (0.5 - 0.5\cos 2t) + \cos 2t\] \[f(t) = 0.5 + 0.5\cos 2t\] Now, we analyze the frequency components of this simplified expression: 1. DC Component (\(0.5\)): A constant term corresponds to an angular frequency \(\omega = 0\,\text{rad/s}\), which means the linear frequency is: \[f_1 = 0\,\text{Hz}\] 2. AC Component (\(0.5\cos 2t\)): Comparing this to the standard form \(A\cos(\omega t)\), the angular frequency is \(\omega = 2\,\text{rad/s}\). The corresponding linear frequency \(f\) is: \[f_2 = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{2}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\text{Hz}\] Therefore, the function \(f(t)\) has frequency components at \(0\) and \(1/\pi\,\text{Hz}\). \[\boxed{\text{(B) f has frequency components at 0 and 1/$\pi$ Hz}}\]
Key points
  • Non-linear terms (like \(\sin^2 t\)) must be expanded using trigonometric identities (e.g., \(\sin^2 \theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}\)) to correctly identify the frequency components of a signal.
  • The relationship between angular frequency (\(\omega\) in rad/s) and linear frequency (\(f\) in Hz) is \(\omega = 2\pi f\).
  • A constant (DC) value in a time-domain signal always corresponds to a frequency of \(0\,\text{Hz}\).

questions.question: Consider a system whose input \(x\) and output \(y\) are related by the equation \[y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t-\tau)h(2\tau)d\tau ,\] where \(h(t)\) is shown in the graph. Which of the following four properties are possessed by the system ? BIBO: Bounded input gives a bounded output. Causal: The system is causal. LP: The system is low pass. LTI: The system is linear and time-invariant.
questions.explanation:
Here \(h(t) \neq 0\) for \(t < 0\). Thus system is non causal. Again any bounded input \(x(t)\) gives bounded output \(y(t)\). Thus it is BIBO stable. Here we can conclude that option (B) is correct. Hence (B) is correct answer. \[\boxed{\text{B) BIBO, LTI }}\]
Key points
  • Causality: An LTI system is causal if and only if its impulse response satisfies \(h(t) = 0\) for all \(t < 0\). If \(h(t) \neq 0\) for any \(t < 0\), the system depends on future inputs and is therefore non-causal.
  • BIBO Stability: A system is Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stable if every bounded input sequence (or signal) produces a bounded output sequence.

questions.question: The Fourier series of a real periodic function has only (P) cosine terms if it is even (Q) sine terms if it is even (R) cosine terms if it is odd (S) sine terms if it is odd Which of the above statements are correct ?
questions.explanation:
The Fourier series of a real periodic function has only cosine terms if it is even and only sine terms if it is odd. Therefore, statement (P) "cosine terms if it is even" and statement (S) "sine terms if it is odd" are correct. \[\boxed{\text{A) P and S }}\]
Key points
  • Even Symmetry: If \(f(t) = f(-t)\), the product \(f(t)\sin(n\omega_0 t)\) is an odd function. Its integral over a fundamental period is zero, making all sine coefficients \(b_n = 0\). The series contains only DC and cosine terms.
  • Odd Symmetry: If \(f(t) = -f(-t)\), the product \(f(t)\cos(n\omega_0 t)\) is an odd function. Its integral over a fundamental period is zero, making the DC component \(a_0 = 0\) and all cosine coefficients \(a_n = 0\). The series contains only sine terms.

questions.question: The ROC of Z-transform of the discrete time sequence \(x(n)= \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(n) - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n u(-n - 1)\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the discrete-time sequence: \[x(n) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(n) - \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n u(-n - 1)\] To find the region of convergence (ROC) of the entire sequence, we analyze the individual terms. The overall ROC is the intersection of the ROCs of the individual terms. Let the first term be \(x_1(n) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^n u(n)\). This is a causal (right-sided) sequence. The standard Z-transform pair is \(a^n u(n) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1 - az^{-1}}\), which converges for \(|z| > |a|\). Therefore, the ROC for \(x_1(n)\) is: \[\text{ROC}_1 : |z| > \frac{1}{3}\] Let the second term be \(x_2(n) = -\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n u(-n - 1)\). This is an anti-causal (left-sided) sequence. The standard Z-transform pair is \(-b^n u(-n - 1) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1 - bz^{-1}}\), which converges for \(|z| < |b|\). Therefore, the ROC for \(x_2(n)\) is: \[\text{ROC}_2 : |z| < \frac{1}{2}\] The overall ROC of \(x(n)\) is the intersection of \(\text{ROC}_1\) and \(\text{ROC}_2\): \[\text{ROC} = \text{ROC}_1 \cap \text{ROC}_2\] \[\text{ROC} = \left( |z| > \frac{1}{3} \right) \cap \left( |z| < \frac{1}{2} \right)\] Combining these conditions yields an annular region in the Z-plane: \[\frac{1}{3} < |z| < \frac{1}{2}\] This matches option A. \[\boxed{\text{A) $\frac{1}{3} < |z| < \frac{1}{2}$ }}\]
Key points
  • For a right-sided sequence \(a^n u(n)\), the ROC is the exterior of a circle of radius \(|a|\), i.e., \(|z| > |a|\).
  • For a left-sided sequence \(-b^n u(-n-1)\), the ROC is the interior of a circle of radius \(|b|\), i.e., \(|z| < |b|\).
  • The ROC of a linear combination of sequences is at least the intersection of their individual ROCs.

questions.question: The 4-point Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) of a discrete time sequence \(\{1, 0, 2, 3\}\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the discrete-time sequence \(x[n] = \{1, 0, 2, 3\}\).
Method 1
Standard DFT Matrix Multiplication
The \(N\)-point Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) is defined as: \[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j\frac{2\pi}{N}nk}\] For \(N = 4\), the computation can be elegantly represented using the \(4 \times 4\) twiddle factor matrix: \[\begin{bmatrix} X[0] \\ X[1] \\ X[2] \\ X[3] \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -j & -1 & j \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & j & -1 & -j \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\] Perform the row-by-column multiplication: \[X[0] = 1(1) + 1(0) + 1(2) + 1(3) = 6\] \[X[1] = 1(1) + (-j)(0) + (-1)(2) + j(3) = 1 - 2 + 3j = -1 + 3j\] \[X[2] = 1(1) + (-1)(0) + 1(2) + (-1)(3) = 1 + 2 - 3 = 0\] \[X[3] = 1(1) + j(0) + (-1)(2) + (-j)(3) = 1 - 2 - 3j = -1 - 3j\] Thus, the complete DFT sequence is \([6, -1 + 3j, 0, -1 - 3j]\).
Method 2
Strategic Elimination
In an examination setting, computing all points is often unnecessary. We can find the purely real components first to quickly eliminate options. The DC component \(X[0]\) is simply the sum of all elements: \[X[0] = \sum_{n=0}^{3} x[n] = 1 + 0 + 2 + 3 = 6\] This immediately eliminates options A and B. Next, compute \(X[2]\), which alternates signs: \[X[2] = \sum_{n=0}^{3} (-1)^n x[n] = 1 - 0 + 2 - 3 = 0\] Looking at the remaining options (C and D), only option D has \(X[2] = 0\). \[\boxed{\text{D) $[6, -1 + 3j, 0, -1 - 3j]$ }}\]
Key points
  • The \(N\)-point DFT evaluates the frequency content of a discrete signal at \(N\) equally spaced frequency points.
  • DC Component: \(X[0] = \sum x[n]\).
  • Nyquist Component (for even \(N\)): \(X[N/2] = \sum (-1)^n x[n]\).
  • Conjugate Symmetry: For a purely real input sequence, \(X[N-k] = X^*[k]\). Here, \(X[3] = X^*[1]\), which holds true since \(-1 - 3j\) is the complex conjugate of \(-1 + 3j\).
Mistakes to avoid
Manually computing complex terms like \(X[1]\) and \(X[3]\) first increases the likelihood of algebraic sign errors involving \(j\). Always compute the purely real sums \(X[0]\) and \(X[N/2]\) first to quickly verify or eliminate multiple-choice options.

questions.question: The ratio of the mobility to the diffusion coefficient in a semiconductor has the units
questions.explanation: The ratio of the diffusion constant \(D\) to the mobility \(\mu\) is equal to the thermal voltage \(V_{T}\): \[\frac{D}{\mu} = V_{T}\] Taking the reciprocal of the above expression, we get the ratio of mobility to the diffusion constant: \[\frac{\mu}{D} = \frac{1}{V_{T}}\] The unit of thermal voltage \(V_{T}\) is Volts (\(\text{V}\)). Therefore, the units for the ratio \(\frac{\mu}{D}\) are: \[\text{units} : \text{V}^{-1}\] \[\boxed{(A) \text{ V}^{-1}}\]

• Silicon atom concentration in Si is about \(5 \times 10^{22},\text{cm}^{-3}\), so A is not possible.
  • In n-type silicon, hole concentration is very small, far below \(4\times10^{19},\text{cm}^{-3}\) , so B is impossible.
  • An n-type Si crystal typically has donor dopant concentration around this order. Thus, C is correct.
  • Each Silicon atom has 4 valence electrons, so the valence electrons concentration is about \(2 \times 10 ^{23} cm^{-3}\), so D is incorrect.

questions.question:
Answer the next two questions using the following data.
Consider a silicon p-n junction at room temperature having the following parameters: Doping on the n-side \(= 1 \times 10^{17}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) Depletion width on the n-side \(= 0.1\,\mu\text{m}\) Depletion width on the p-side \(= 1.0\,\mu\text{m}\) Intrinsic carrier concentration \(= 1.4 \times 10^{10}\text{ cm}^{-3}\) Thermal voltage \(= 26\text{ mV}\) Permittivity of free space \(= 8.85 \times 10^{-14}\text{ F} \text{cm}^{-1}\) Dielectric constant of silicon \(= 12\)

The peak electric field in the device is
options: \(0.15\text{ MV} \text{cm}^{-1}\), directed from p-region to n-region
\(0.15\text{ MV} \text{cm}^{-1}\), directed from n-region to p-region
\(1.80\text{ MV} \text{cm}^{-1}\), directed from p-region to n-region

Given \(h_{ie}=r_\pi = 3\text{ K}\Omega\), \(\beta = 150\) and \[v_i(t) = A\cos 20t + B\sin 10^6t\] Given circuit is, The input signal \(v_i(t)\) consists of two frequency components: \(A \cos 20t\) (low frequency) and \(B \sin 10^6t\) (high frequency). The common emitter circuit given has a coupling capacitor at input and at output. The presence of \(100\,\text{nF}\) coupling capacitors and a \(10\,\mu\text{F}\) bypass capacitor acts as a high-pass filter, blocking low-frequency signals. Therefore, the amplifier will only pass significant high-frequency components. At very low frequency, the capacitive reactance is high, and input is blocked, so the \(A \cos 20t\) component is heavily attenuated. At high frequency, the capacitive reactance is low and \(B \sin 10^6t\) passes through and gets amplified. AC Analysis : The AC equivalent circuit is given by deactivating DC sources, shorting capacitors and replacing bjt with its small signal model. Applying KVL in input and output loops, \[V_i = h_{ie}i_b\] \[V_0 = -\beta i_bR_C\] Amplifier voltage gain: \[A_v = \frac{V_0}{V_i}=- \frac{\beta \cdot R_C}{h_{ie}}\] \[A_v = - \frac{150 \times 3000}{3000}\] \[A_v = -150\] Only the \(B \sin 10^6t\) term will appear at the output, multiplied by the gain \(-150\): \[v_o(t) = A_V\times V_i(t)=-150 \times B \sin 10^6t\] \[\boxed{\text{(D)\quad}v_o(t) = -150 B \sin 10^6t}\]

questions.question:
If \(X = 1\) in the logic equation
\(\left[ X + Z \left\{ \overline{Y} + \left( \overline{Z} + X\overline{Y} \right) \right\} \right] \left\{ \overline{X} + \overline{Z} \left( X + Y \right) \right\} = 1\), then
questions.explanation:
Given the Boolean logic equation: \[\left[ X + Z \left\{ \overline{Y} + \left( \overline{Z} + X\,\overline{Y} \right) \right\} \right] \left\{ \overline{X} + \overline{Z} \left( X + Y \right) \right\} = 1\] Substituting the given condition \(X = 1\) (which implies \(\overline{X} = 0\)) into the equation:
  • First term simplification:
    \[\left[ 1 + Z \left\{ \overline{Y} + \left( \overline{Z} + 1 \cdot \overline{Y} \right) \right\} \right] = 1 \quad (\because 1 + \text{any expression} = 1)\]
  • Second term simplification:
    \[\left\{ 0 + \overline{Z} \left( 1 + Y \right) \right\} = \left\{ \overline{Z} \cdot 1 \right\} = \overline{Z} \quad (\because 1 + Y = 1)\]
Combining the simplified terms back into the original equation: \[[1] \cdot \left[ \overline{Z} \right] = 1 \implies \overline{Z} = 1 \implies Z = 0\] \[\boxed{\text{(D) } Z = 0}\]
Key points
  • Annihilation Law: \(1 + A = 1\)
  • Identity Law: \(1 \cdot A = A\)

  • If only \(P_1\) is pressed, `2' is displayed, signifying `Rs. 2'.

To comprehensively analyze the circuit, we derive the minimized Boolean expressions for all 7 segments (\(a\) through \(g\)) using the truth table:

  2. Segment \(b\): It is \(1\) at rows 0 and 2. \[b = \overline{P_1}\,\overline{P_2} + P_1\overline{P_2} = (\overline{P_1} + P_1)\overline{P_2} = 1 \cdot \overline{P_2} = \overline{P_2}\]
  3. Segment \(c\): It is \(1\) at rows 0 and 1. \[c = \overline{P_1}\,\overline{P_2} + \overline{P_1}P_2 = \overline{P_1}(\overline{P_2} + P_2) = \overline{P_1} \cdot 1 = \overline{P_1}\]
  4. Segment \(d\): It is \(1\) for all input combinations. \[d = 1\]
  5. Segment \(e\): It is \(1\) at rows 0, 2, and 3. \[e = \overline{P_1}\,\overline{P_2} + P_1\overline{P_2} + P_1P_2 = (\overline{P_1} + P_1)\overline{P_2} + P_1P_2 = \overline{P_2} + P_1P_2\] Applying the distributive property (\(X + \overline{X}Y = X + Y\)): \[e = \overline{P_2} + P_1\]

What are the minimum number of 2-to-1 multiplexers required to generate a 2-input AND gate and a 2-input Ex-OR gate ?
questions.explanation:
To determine the minimum number of \(2 \times 1\) multiplexers (MUX) required to generate a 2-input AND gate and a 2-input Ex-OR gate, we analyze each logic function separately:
  1. Implementation of a 2-input AND gate (\(Y = AB\)):
    The output equation of a standard \(2 \times 1\) MUX with selection line \(S\) is: \[Y = \overline{S}I_0 + SI_1\] By choosing the selection line \(S = A\), and assigning fixed inputs \(I_0 = 0\) and \(I_1 = B\): \[Y = \overline{A}\cdot 0 + A\cdot B = AB\] Thus, exactly 1, \(2 \times 1\) MUX is required to implement a 2-input AND gate.
  2. Implementation of a 2-input Ex-OR gate (\(Y = A\oplus B = \overline{A}B + A\overline{B}\)):
    Using a standard \(2 \times 1\) MUX with selection line \(S = A\): \[Y = \overline{A}I_0 + AI_1\] Comparing this with the Ex-OR expression, we require \(I_0 = B\) and \(I_1 = \overline{B}\). Since the complemented literal \(\overline{B}\) is not directly available, we must generate it using another \(2 \times 1\) MUX configured as an inverter: \[Y_1 = \overline{B}\cdot 1 + B\cdot 0 = \overline{B}\] This inverter MUX uses \(S = B\), \(I_0 = 1\), and \(I_1 = 0\). Feeding its output \(Y_1 = \overline{B}\) into input \(I_1\) of the first MUX gives the complete Ex-OR function. Thus, exactly 2 \(2 \times 1\) MUXs are required to implement a 2-input Ex-OR gate.
Therefore, the minimum number of \(2 \times 1\) multiplexers needed is 1 and 2, respectively. \[\boxed{\text{(A) 1 and 2}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that complements like \(\overline{B}\) are freely available unless explicitly stated in the problem statement. Always account for the extra MUX required for inversion.

questions.question: Refer to the NAND and NOR latches shown in the figure. The inputs \((P_1, P_2)\) for both the latches are first made \((0,1)\) and then, after a few seconds, made \((1,1)\). The corresponding stable outputs \((Q_1, Q_2)\) are
questions.explanation:
The circuit consists of cross-coupled latches analyzed sequentially under two input configurations: first \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (0, 1)\), then transitioning to \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (1, 1)\). 1. NAND Latch Analysis Case 1: \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (0, 1)\) Since \(P_1 = 0\), the top NAND gate forces \(Q_1 = 1\). Feeding this back with \(P_2 = 1\) yields: \[Q_2 = \overline{P_2 \cdot Q_1} = \overline{1 \cdot 1} = 0\] Thus, the stable output state is \((Q_1, Q_2) = (1, 0)\). Case 2: Transition to \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (1, 1)\) The input \((1, 1)\) is the hold state for a NAND latch, keeping the prior outputs unchanged. Thus, the stable state remains \((Q_1, Q_2) = (1, 0)\). 2. NOR Latch Analysis Case 1: \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (0, 1)\) Since \(P_2 = 1\), the bottom NOR gate forces \(Q_2 = 0\). Feeding this back with \(P_1 = 0\) yields: \[Q_1 = \overline{P_1 + Q_2} = \overline{0 + 0} = 1\] Thus, the stable output state is \((Q_1, Q_2) = (1, 0)\). Case 2: Transition to \((P_{1}, P_{2}) = (1, 1)\) With both inputs high, both NOR gates are forced low simultaneously regardless of feedback: \[Q_1 = \overline{1 + 0} = 0, \quad Q_2 = \overline{1 + 0} = 0\] Hence, the subsequent stable state changes to \((Q_1, Q_2) = (0, 0)\). Combining these sequential transitions matches the evaluations described in choice (C). \[\boxed{\text{(C) NAND: first (1, 0) then (1, 0); NOR: first (1, 0) then (0, 0)}}\]
Key points
  • For a NAND latch, if any input is 0, its output instantly becomes 1 without waiting for the other input.
  • Similarly, for a NOR latch, if any input is 1, its output instantly becomes 0.
  • The state \((1,1)\) represents a memory hold configuration for a NAND latch, but acts as an invalid/cleared drive condition for a NOR latch.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that \((1,1)\) acts as a hold state for both configurations; make sure to evaluate the deterministic output based on basic gate properties first.

questions.explanation:
To identify the type of interrupt described, let's analyze its characteristics based on how it handles addresses and execution controls:
  1. Vectored vs. Non-Vectored (Address Location):
    • The problem states that the service routine starts from a fixed location of memory which cannot be externally altered.
    • When an interrupt has a predefined, hardwired memory address for its execution routine, it is classified as a vectored interrupt.
  2. Maskable vs. Non-Maskable (Delay or Rejection Control):
    • The problem states that the interrupt can be delayed or rejected by the processor.
    • If the processor has the authority to ignore, disable, or postpone an incoming request, the interrupt is classified as a maskable interrupt.
Combining both properties, the interrupt is both maskable and vectored, which aligns with option (D). \[\boxed{\text{(D) maskable and vectored}}\]
Key points
  • Vectored Interrupt: Automatically points the Program Counter to a fixed vector address table entry without requiring external address inputs.
  • Maskable Interrupt: Can be enabled or disabled via soft-setting internal status register bits (like the Interrupt Enable flag).

questions.question: The feedback configuration and the pole-zero locations of \(G(s) = \dfrac{s^2 - 2s + 2}{s^2 + 2s + 2}\) are shown below. The root locus for negative values of \(K\), i.e. for \(-\infty < K < 0\), has breakaway/break-in points and angle of departure at pole \(P\) (with respect to the positive real axis) equal to
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of the closed-loop system is: \[1 + K G(s) H(s) = 0 \implies 1 + K \frac{s^2 - 2s + 2}{s^2 + 2s + 2} = 0\] \[K = -\frac{s^2 + 2s + 2}{s^2 - 2s + 2}\] Setting \(\dfrac{\partial K}{\partial s} = 0\) for breakaway/break-in points: \[\frac{\partial K}{\partial s} = -\frac{(2s + 2)(s^2 - 2s + 2) - (2s - 2)(s^2 + 2s + 2)}{(s^2 - 2s + 2)^2} = 0\] \[(s^3 - s^2 + 2) - (s^3 + s^2 - 2) = 0 \implies \boxed{s = \pm\sqrt{2}}\] img/ch5_root_locus/5_09_1.png Note: The original problem's pole-zero plot layout is incorrect. Zeros are at \(s = 1 \pm j\) and poles are at \(s = -1 \pm j\). The angular contributions to complex pole \(P = -1 + j\) are:
  • From pole \(P^* = -1 - j \implies \phi_{p1} = 90^\circ\)
  • From zero \(Z_1 = 1 + j \implies \phi_{z1} = 180^\circ\)
  • From zero \(Z_2 = 1 - j \implies \phi_{z2} = 180^\circ - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{2}\right) = 135^\circ\)
For a negative root locus (\(K < 0\)), the phase criteria equals \(0^\circ\) (or even multiples of \(180^\circ\)).
Method 1
Using phasor phase angle method for \(K < 0\): \[\phi_{D} = 0^\circ + \angle G(s)H(s) \Big|_{s = -1+j}\] \[\angle G(s)H(s) = (\phi_{z1} + \phi_{z2}) - \phi_{p1}\] \[\angle G(s)H(s) = (180^\circ + 135^\circ) - 90^\circ = 225^\circ\] \[\phi_{D} = 0^\circ + 225^\circ = 225^\circ \equiv -135^\circ\]
Method 2
Using explicit summation method for \(K < 0\): \[\phi_{D} = 0^\circ - \phi \quad \left[\text{where } \phi = \sum \phi_{p'} - \sum \phi_{z}\right]\] \[\phi = \phi_{p1} - (\phi_{z1} + \phi_{z2})\] \[\phi = 90^\circ - (180^\circ + 135^\circ) = -225^\circ\] \[\phi_{D} = 0^\circ - (-225^\circ) = 225^\circ \equiv -135^\circ\]
No option matches \(\boxed{\phi_{D} = -135^\circ \text{ or } 225^\circ}\).
Mistakes to avoid
For a negative root locus (\(K < 0\)), the baseline reference angle factor switches from \(180^\circ\) to \(0^\circ\).

Theory: The power spectral density and autocorrelation function form a Fourier transform pair (Wiener--Khinchin theorem). Key points

questions.question: A white noise process \(X(t)\) with two-sided power spectral density \[S_X(f)=1\times 10^{-10}\ \text{W/Hz}\]is input to a filter whose magnitude-squared response \(|H(f)|^2\) is triangular, having\[|H(0)|^2 = 1,\]and extending from\(-10\,\text{kHz} \le f \le 10\,\text{kHz}.\)The power of the output process \(Y(t)\) is
questions.explanation: Theory: For a white noise input, the output PSD is obtained by multiplying the input PSD with the filter magnitude-squared response: \[S_Y(f)=|H(f)|^2S_X(f).\]The output power is the area under the output PSD. Given,\[S_X(f)=1\times 10^{-10}\ \text{W/Hz}.\]Let\[k=1\times 10^{-10}\ \text{W/Hz}.\]Hence, \[S_Y(f)=k|H(f)|^2.\]The output power is\[P_Y = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_Y(f)\,df = k\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^2\,df.\]Since \(|H(f)|^2\) is a triangle with \[\text{height}=1\]and \[\text{base}=20\,\text{kHz}=2\times10^4\ \text{Hz},\]its area is \[A = \frac{1}{2}\times \text{base}\times \text{height}\] \[= \frac{1}{2}\times(2\times10^4)\times1\] \[= 10^4.\]Therefore, \[P_Y = kA = (10^{-10})(10^4)\] \[= 10^{-6}\ \text{W}.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(B) P_Y=1\times10^{-6}\ \text{W}}\]

Answer the question 2.09.1 and question 2.09.2 using the following data. The amplitude of a random signal is uniformly distributed between \(-5\ \text{V}\) and \(5\ \text{V}\).

If the signal to quantization noise ratio required in uniformly quantizing the signal is \(43.5\ \text{dB}\), the step size of the quantization is approximately
questions.explanation: Theory: For a uniform quantizer, the quantization noise power is \[N_0=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\]The SQNR is defined as the ratio of signal power to quantization noise power. The random signal is uniformly distributed over the interval \[-5 \le x \le 5.\]Hence, its probability density function is \[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{10}, \qquad -5 \le x \le 5.\]The signal power is \[S=E[X^2] =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^2f_X(x)\,dx\] \[=\int_{-5}^{5}\frac{1}{10}x^2\,dx\] \[=\frac{1}{10} \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-5}^{5}\] \[=\frac{1}{10} \left(\frac{125}{3}+\frac{125}{3}\right)\] \[=\frac{25}{3}.\]Given, \[\mathrm{SQNR}=43.5\ \text{dB}.\]Converting into linear scale, \[\mathrm{SQNR} = 10^{43.5/10} = 10^{4.35}.\]Since \[\mathrm{SQNR} = \frac{S}{N_0},\]and \[N_0=\frac{\Delta^2}{12},\]we get \[\frac{\Delta^2}{12} = \frac{S}{\mathrm{SQNR}}.\]Therefore, \[\Delta = \sqrt{\frac{12S}{\mathrm{SQNR}}}.\]Substituting the values, \[\Delta = \sqrt{ \frac{12\left(\frac{25}{3}\right)} {10^{4.35}} }.\] \[= \sqrt{ \frac{100} {10^{4.35}} }.\] \[\Delta \approx 0.0668\ \text{V}.\]Hence, \[\boxed{(C)\Delta \approx 0.0667\ \text{V}}\]

questions.question:
Answer the question 2.09.1 and question 2.09.2 using the following data. The amplitude of a random signal is uniformly distributed between \(-5\ \text{V}\) and \(5\ \text{V}\).

If the positive values of the signal are uniformly quantized with a step size of \(0.05\ \text{V}\), and the negative values are uniformly quantized with a step size of \(0.1\ \text{V}\), the resulting signal to quantization noise ratio is approximately
questions.explanation: Theory: Quantization noise power for a uniform quantizer is \[\sigma_q^2=\frac{\Delta^2}{12}.\]Since the positive and negative halves use different step sizes, the overall quantization noise power is the probability-weighted average of the two noise powers. Given, \[\Delta_1 = 0.05\ \text{V} \qquad \text{(for positive values)}\] \[\Delta_2 = 0.1\ \text{V} \qquad \text{(for negative values)}\]Since the signal amplitude is uniformly distributed between \(-5\) V and \(5\) V, \[P(\Delta_1)=P(\Delta_2)=\frac{1}{2}.\]Hence, the quantization noise power is \[N_0 = \frac{\Delta_1^2}{12}P(\Delta_1) + \frac{\Delta_2^2}{12}P(\Delta_2)\] \[= \frac{1}{24} \left( \Delta_1^2+\Delta_2^2 \right)\] \[= \frac{1}{24} \left( 0.05^2+0.1^2 \right)\] \[= \frac{1}{24} \left( 0.0025+0.01 \right)\] \[= \frac{0.0125}{24} = \frac{125}{24\times 10000} = \frac{1}{1920}.\]The signal power of a uniformly distributed random variable over \([-5,5]\) is \[S = E[X^2] = \frac{A^2}{3} = \frac{5^2}{3} = \frac{25}{3}.\]Therefore, \[\mathrm{SQNR} = \frac{S}{N_0} = \frac{\frac{25}{3}}{\frac{1}{1920}} = \frac{1920\times 25}{3} = 16000.\]In decibels, \[\mathrm{SQNR}_{dB} = 10\log_{10}(16000)\] \[= 42.04\ \text{dB}.\] \[\boxed{(C) \mathrm{SQNR}\approx 42\ \text{dB}}\]

questions.question: A communication channel with AWGN operating at a signal-to-noise ratio \[\mathrm{SNR} \gg 1\]and bandwidth \(B\) has capacity \(C_1\). If the SNR is doubled while keeping the bandwidth constant, the resulting capacity \(C_2\) is given by
questions.explanation:
Theory: For an AWGN channel, Shannon capacity is \[C = B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}).\]Since \[\mathrm{SNR}\gg 1,\]we can use the approximation \[1+\mathrm{SNR}\approx \mathrm{SNR}.\]Therefore, \[C_1 = B\log_2(\mathrm{SNR}).\]When the SNR is doubled, \[\mathrm{SNR}'=2\,\mathrm{SNR}.\]Hence, \[C_2 = B\log_2(2\,\mathrm{SNR}).\]Using the logarithmic property \[\log_2(ab)=\log_2 a+\log_2 b,\]we obtain \[C_2 = B\left[\log_2 2+\log_2(\mathrm{SNR})\right].\]Since \[\log_2 2 = 1,\] \[C_2 = B+B\log_2(\mathrm{SNR}).\]But \[C_1=B\log_2(\mathrm{SNR}),\]therefore \[\boxed{(B) C_2 \approx C_1+B}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Capacity is proportional to the logarithm of SNR, not directly proportional to SNR: \[C=B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}).\]Doubling SNR does not double capacity.
  • For high SNR, \[1+\mathrm{SNR}\approx \mathrm{SNR},\]which greatly simplifies the calculation.
  • The result \[C_2=C_1+B\]is valid only under the approximation \[\mathrm{SNR}\gg 1.\]

questions.question: A message signal given by \[m(t)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\cos\omega_1t-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\sin\omega_2t\]is amplitude-modulated with a carrier of frequency \(\omega_c\) to generate \[s(t)=\left[1+m(t)\right]\cos\omega_ct\]What is the power efficiency achieved by this modulation scheme?
questions.explanation:
Theory: For a multi-tone AM signal, the overall modulation index is obtained by the root-sum-square of the individual modulation indices, and the transmission efficiency is \[\eta=\frac{m_a^2}{2+m_a^2}\times100\%.\]Given, \[m(t)=\left(\frac12\right)\cos\omega_1t-\left(\frac12\right)\sin\omega_2t.\]Hence, \[m_{a1}=\frac12,\qquad m_{a2}=\frac12.\]Therefore, the equivalent modulation index is \[m_a=\sqrt{m_{a1}^2+m_{a2}^2} =\sqrt{\left(\frac12\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2} =\sqrt{\frac12}.\]Thus, \[m_a^2=\frac12.\]The power efficiency is \[\eta = \frac{m_a^2}{2+m_a^2}\times100\% = \frac{\frac12}{2+\frac12}\times100\% = \frac{0.5}{2.5}\times100\% = 20\%.\] \[\boxed{(C) \eta=20\%}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not add the modulation indices directly; use the root-sum-square for multiple independent tones.
  • Do not forget that the efficiency formula uses \(m_a^2\), not \(m_a\).
  • Compute the equivalent modulation index first, then substitute it into the efficiency formula.
  • Do not confuse transmission efficiency with modulation index.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the fundamental mode of the metallic waveguides shown? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
This problem contrasts the fundamental electromagnetic wave propagation characteristics in coaxial lines versus waveguides.
  • Coaxial Line (\(P\)): A coaxial cable supports the Transverse Electromagnetic (TEM) mode as its dominant mode. Because the TEM mode does not require specific boundary conditions related to a cutoff frequency, a coaxial line can theoretically transmit signals from DC (zero frequency) up to an upper limit defined by higher-order mode excitation. Thus, it has no lower cutoff frequency.
  • Waveguides (\(Q\) and \(R\)): In contrast, hollow metallic waveguides operate by supporting Transverse Electric (TE) or Transverse Magnetic (TM) modes. These modes are subject to boundary conditions that require the frequency to be above a specific cutoff frequency, \(f_{c}\), determined by the physical dimensions of the waveguide.
\[f_{c} \propto \frac{1}{\text{Dimensions}}\] \[\boxed{(A):\text{Only $P$ has no cut-off frequency.}}\]
Key points
  • TEM waves exist in transmission lines with two or more conductors (e.g., coaxial, parallel plate).
